header.title: Datacenter moratoriums barely dent the US AI buildout pipeline

s01_bottom_line.text: SemiAnalysis's parcel-level audit finds that 300+ local moratoriums and NY's order delay only ~2.3GW genuinely, with just 1,525 MW (7.6% of restricted-boundary capacity) delayed at the local level, against a +38GW 2027 US delivery forecast. ⟨cited figures: approximate; forecast⟩
The article concludes the buildout is not being legislated to a halt; capacity under construction or permitted for 2026 and most of 2027 is out of reach of moratoriums.

The moratorium narrative appears materially overstated as a near-term risk to datacenter capacity and the AI infrastructure supply chain, though the article quantifies no specific listed-company earnings or revenue effect.

alternative_mechanisms.text: The widespread media narrative holds that moratoriums are killing the US datacenter buildout, legislated to a halt one board at a time.
Public sentiment is significantly negative on datacenters (46% unfavorable) and could intensify opposition, potentially widening restrictions over time.

counter_evidence.text: 46% of voters view datacenters unfavorably (24% very unfavorably) vs 29% favorable
46% would oppose a new datacenter in their own city/town (30% strongly oppose)
SemiAnalysis view: moratoriums could delay the buildout but are not yet at scale
In May 2026, Howell Township's board voted to extend its datacenter moratorium for an additional six months.

disconfirming_observables.text: A sharp rise in enacted statewide moratoriums reaching floor votes
Revocation (not just freezing) of already-granted datacenter approvals
Upward revision to SemiAnalysis's genuinely-delayed GW estimate

market_risks.text: Public sentiment is significantly negative on datacenters (46% unfavorable, 46% would oppose one locally), and SemiAnalysis warns this gap could widen with AI doomsday narratives, potentially making moratoriums materially more widespread and restrictive. (scope: US voter sentiment per SemiAnalysis's August 2026 Tokenomics survey; the article says moratoriums are not yet at scale but could delay the buildout if they become more widespread.)

Election-year politics (November 2026 midterms) could raise the political cost of approving datacenter projects, as candidates like Vivek Ramaswamy pledge strict conditions, potentially catalyzing new restrictions. (scope: US state and local campaigns; the article frames this as a catalyst for new restrictions rather than an established delay to capacity.)

Regional clustering can make local moratorium activity self-reinforcing, with opposition arguments, advocacy groups, model ordinance language and political pressure spreading quickly among neighboring jurisdictions. (scope: Local datacenter moratoriums in regions experiencing rapid datacenter growth (e.g. Metro Atlanta); presented as a potential, not realized, escalation.)

unknowns.text: Whether moratoriums become materially more widespread and restrictive, which the article says would be needed to delay the buildout
Whether any listed hyperscaler or datacenter supplier earnings/revenue actually change as a result
Whether the parcel-level exposure-vs-delay mapping holds for 2028+ projects not yet permitted
